text: Earth's mean diameter is 12,742 kilometres
source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Earth Fact Sheet (volumetric mean radius 6,371 km)

text: Doubling Earth's radius gives a diameter of about 25,500 kilometres
source: Arithmetic from NASA Earth Fact Sheet radius of 6,371 km

text: Earth's mean density is about 5.5 times that of water
as_written: about five and a half times that of water
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (5,514 kg per cubic metre)

text: Seven additional Earths of material are needed to double radius at constant density, since mass scales as radius cubed
as_written: you would need seven more Earths of material
source: Arithmetic: volume scales with radius cubed, 2 cubed is 8

text: A rocky planet of eight Earth masses has a radius of about 1.8 Earth radii for Earth-like composition
as_written: around 1.8 times Earth's width by the usual models
source: Zeng, Sasselov and Jacobsen 2016, Astrophysical Journal, mass-radius relation for Earth-like rocky planets (R roughly proportional to M^0.27); Seager et al. 2007, Astrophysical Journal

text: Earth's surface area is about 510 million square kilometres
source: NOAA / USGS Earth surface area figure (510.1 million square km)

text: Surface area grows four times when radius doubles, to over two billion square kilometres
source: Arithmetic: 4 times 510 million is about 2.04 billion square km

text: Volume and mass grow eight times at constant density; surface gravity scales as mass over radius squared, giving a factor of two
as_written: eight divided by four. Exactly double
source: Newton's law of gravitation, g = GM/R squared

text: Earth's surface gravity is about 9.8 metres per second squared
as_written: about 9.8 metres per second, every second
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (9.80 m/s2); CGPM standard gravity 9.80665 m/s2

text: Doubled gravity gives 19.6 metres per second squared
source: Arithmetic from NASA Earth Fact Sheet value

text: Fighter pilots with anti-g suits train for about nine g
source: US Air Force / NASA aerospace physiology literature on high-G training (9 g centrifuge standard)

text: Untrained people typically lose vision or consciousness between about four and six g
source: NASA and USAF aerospace medicine references on G-induced loss of consciousness

text: Fall time from one metre is about 0.45 seconds on Earth and 0.32 seconds at double gravity
source: Kinematics, t = sqrt(2h/g), using g = 9.8 and 19.6 m/s2

text: Impact speed from a one metre fall is 4.4 metres per second on Earth and 6.3 at double gravity
source: Kinematics, v = sqrt(2gh)

text: Impact energy per kilogram doubles at double gravity from the same height
source: Energy per unit mass = g times h

text: Jump height with the same take-off speed halves at double gravity
source: Kinematics, h = v squared over 2g

text: Horizon distance for eye height 1.7 m is about 4.7 km on Earth and about 6.6 km at double radius
source: Geometry, d = sqrt(2Rh), using R = 6,371 km

text: Atmospheric mass scaled by eight over four times the area under twice gravity gives four atmospheres
source: Hydrostatic balance, P = M_atm g / (4 pi R squared); arithmetic 8 x 2 / 4

text: Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly one atmosphere, so four atmospheres corresponds to about thirty metres depth
as_written: about thirty metres under the surface
source: NOAA Diving Manual; US Navy Diving Manual (33 feet of seawater per atmosphere)

text: Nitrogen narcosis typically begins around 30 metres depth
as_written: about the depth at which many divers start to report nitrogen narcosis
source: US Navy Diving Manual; Divers Alert Network

text: Air is about 21 percent oxygen
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet / standard atmosphere composition

text: At four atmospheres, oxygen partial pressure is about 0.84 atmospheres, equivalent to 84 percent oxygen at sea level
source: Dalton's law; arithmetic 0.21 x 4

text: Prolonged exposure to oxygen above roughly 0.5 atmospheres risks pulmonary oxygen toxicity
source: NOAA Diving Manual, pulmonary oxygen toxicity and OTU model; Clark and Lambertsen

text: Sea-level air density is about 1.2 kilograms per cubic metre
source: International Standard Atmosphere (1.225 kg/m3), ICAO

text: Wind force on an object scales with air density, so four times denser air gives four times the force at the same speed
source: Aerodynamic drag equation, F = 0.5 rho v squared C A

text: Atmospheric scale height on Earth is about 8.5 kilometres and halves at double gravity to about 4.2
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (scale height 8.5 km); scale height H = kT/mg

text: Solar irradiance at Earth's distance is about 1,361 watts per square metre
source: NASA SORCE / Total Irradiance Monitor, total solar irradiance 1361 W/m2 (Kopp and Lean 2011)

text: Earth rotates once in about 24 hours
source: IERS; NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Earth's orbital period is about 365 days
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Earth's mean orbital speed is about 29.8 kilometres per second
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (29.78 km/s)

text: The Sun outweighs eight Earth masses by more than forty thousand times
source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet (Sun about 333,000 Earth masses); 333,000 divided by 8 is about 41,600

text: Earth's equatorial rotation speed is about 1,670 kilometres per hour
source: Computed from NASA Earth Fact Sheet equatorial radius 6,378 km and sidereal rotation period 23.93 h

text: At double radius with the same rotation, equatorial speed is about 3,350 kilometres per hour
source: Arithmetic: 2 x 1,674 km/h

text: The Moon's mean distance is 384,400 kilometres
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: The Moon's orbital period is 27.3 days
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (sidereal period 27.32 days)

text: With eight times the central mass the Moon's period at the same distance falls to a little under ten days
source: Kepler's third law, period proportional to 1 over sqrt(mass); 27.3 / 2.8 is about 9.7

text: Geostationary altitude is 35,786 kilometres
source: NASA / ESA geostationary orbit specification

text: With eight times the mass, geostationary orbital radius doubles, giving an altitude of about 71,600 km above a planet of radius 12,742 km
source: Kepler's third law, r proportional to (M T squared) to the one third; 2 x 42,164 km minus 12,742 km

text: A ground-skimming circular orbit takes about 84 minutes on Earth and the same on the doubled planet
source: Kepler's third law, T = 2 pi sqrt(R cubed / GM); about 84.4 minutes using NASA Earth Fact Sheet values

text: Circular orbital speed at the surface is about 7.9 km/s on Earth and about 15.8 km/s on the doubled planet
source: Orbital mechanics, v = sqrt(GM/R); NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: At four atmospheres water boils at about 144 degrees Celsius
source: IAPWS-IF97 steam tables, saturation temperature at 405 kPa about 143.6 C

text: The tallest known living tree, Hyperion, is about 116 metres tall
source: US National Park Service / Redwood National Park; Hyperion measured 115.92 m

text: The hydraulic limit to tree height on Earth is around 120 to 130 metres
source: Koch et al. 2004, Nature, The limits to tree height

text: Four times density at the same speed gives four times lift; stall speed scales with sqrt(weight over density), so it falls by about 30 percent at double weight and four times density
source: Standard aerodynamic lift equation and stall speed relation; sqrt(2/4) = 0.71

text: Earth loses about 47 terawatts of heat through its surface
source: Davies and Davies 2010, Solid Earth, Earth's surface heat flux

text: Interior heat production scales with volume (eight times) while surface area scales four times
as_written: eight times while the second goes up four
source: Geometry: volume scales with radius cubed, area with radius squared

text: Researchers disagree on whether super-Earths have plate tectonics
as_written: One group of researchers in 2007 argued
source: Valencia, O'Connell and Sasselov 2007, Icarus; O'Neill and Lenardic 2007, Geophysical Research Letters

text: Earth's escape velocity is about 11.2 kilometres per second, doubling to about 22.4 at double radius and eight times mass
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (11.186 km/s); v_esc proportional to sqrt(M/R)

text: Hydrogen-oxygen rocket engines have exhaust speed of about 4.4 kilometres per second
source: Aerojet Rocketdyne RS-25 specific impulse about 452 s in vacuum; v_e = Isp x g0

text: Each additional exhaust velocity of delta-v multiplies propellant mass ratio by e, about 2.7
source: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation

text: Reaching low Earth orbit needs a delta-v of about 9.4 kilometres per second including losses
source: NASA launch vehicle performance references; Wertz and Larson, Space Mission Analysis and Design

text: Orbital speed on the doubled planet is about 16 km/s before losses
source: Orbital mechanics, 2 x 7.9 km/s

text: Ideal single-stage mass ratios are about 8 for Earth and about 37 for the doubled planet
as_written: about eight, and one of around thirty-seven
source: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation with delta-v 9.4 and 16 km/s and exhaust speed 4.4 km/s

text: A 2018 study found spaceflight from super-Earths is sharply harder
as_written: A 2018 study by the astronomer Michael Hippke
source: Hippke 2018, Spaceflight from Super-Earths is difficult, arXiv:1804.04886; International Journal of Astrobiology 2019

text: Everest is 8,849 metres high
source: Nepal and China joint survey announced December 2020

text: Mars surface gravity is about 3.7 metres per second squared
source: NASA Mars Fact Sheet (3.73 m/s2)

text: Olympus Mons rises about 21.9 kilometres
source: NASA / USGS Mars MOLA topography (Olympus Mons about 21.9 km above datum)

text: Ratio of Olympus Mons to Everest height is about 2.5 and ratio of Earth to Mars gravity is about 2.6
source: Arithmetic from the figures above: 21.9 / 8.85; 9.8 / 3.73

text: Maximum mountain height scales inversely with gravity, giving roughly half of Earth's height, about four and a half kilometres, at double gravity
as_written: perhaps four and a half kilometres
source: Isostatic and rock-strength limits on relief; Melosh, Planetary Surface Processes (2011)

text: Earth's oceans hold about 1.3 billion cubic kilometres
source: USGS Water Science School; NOAA (about 1.335 billion cubic km)

text: Spread over a smooth Earth, the oceans would be about 2.6 kilometres deep
source: Arithmetic: 1.335 billion cubic km divided by 510 million square km

text: Eight times the water over four times the area gives twice the depth, about 5.2 km
source: Arithmetic: 2 x 2.6 km

text: Earth's oceans are about 0.02 percent of its mass
source: Ocean mass about 1.4e21 kg (NOAA / USGS) divided by Earth mass 5.97e24 kg (NASA Earth Fact Sheet)

text: Planet sizes show a gap between about 1.5 and 2 Earth radii
as_written: common below about 1.5 times Earth's radius and common above about 2
source: Fulton et al. 2017, Astronomical Journal, California-Kepler Survey radius gap

text: Most planets larger than about 1.6 Earth radii are not rocky
as_written: larger than about 1.6 times Earth's radius
source: Rogers 2015, Astrophysical Journal, Most 1.6 Earth-radius planets are not rocky

text: 55 Cancri e has a radius about 1.9 Earth radii and a mass about eight Earth masses
as_written: a radius about 1.9 times Earth's and a mass about eight times Earth's
source: Bourrier et al. 2018, Astronomy and Astrophysics (7.99 Earth masses, 1.88 Earth radii)

text: 55 Cancri e orbits its star in less than a day
source: Winn et al. 2011, Astrophysical Journal Letters (orbital period 0.74 days)
